There is a particular kind of silence that arrives after rain. Not the silence of absence, but the silence of something completed—the earth exhaling, the leaves still holding the weight of water, each drop occasionally slipping loose to tap the pavement below. I like to stand in that moment, when the world feels freshly made, and listen to the small sounds: the distant rush of a gutter, the soft patter of a branch shaking free, the way even the air sounds different—wet and green and patient.

I have been thinking about attention lately. How much of our lives passes through us without actually touching us. We scroll, we rush, we plan the next thing while doing the present thing. We are always somewhere else in our heads. But then, sometimes, a moment snaps into focus: a shaft of afternoon light cutting across a dusty room, the smell of bread from a doorway, a stranger’s laugh echoing in a narrow street. And for just a second, we are fully there. Not thinking. Not wanting. Just being.

It reminds me of something a friend once said: that we don’t remember days, we remember moments. The hours blur together, but a single instant—sharp and glowing—can carry the whole weight of a summer. I think she was right. The mind is not a camera that saves everything. It is more like an old house, with only a few rooms kept open, and the rest sealed shut. The moments we keep are the ones we truly paid attention to.

Why is it so hard, then? Why do we drift? Perhaps because attention is a kind of courage. To really look at something means to be affected by it. To hear someone fully means to risk being changed. We protect ourselves by skimming, by staying at the surface, by keeping one foot out the door. But that protection comes at a cost. The walls of the sealed rooms grow thicker. The colors of the world dull. We become ghosts in our own lives, haunting the edges of experience.

I want to live more awake. To feel the texture of things. To taste the salt and the sweet. To let the world leave marks on me. I want to be someone who stops, not because there is time, but because there is meaning in stopping. The Japanese have a word, *komorebi*—the light that filters through the leaves of trees. There is something in that word that captures it: the beauty of what is partial, broken, filtered. Not the full sun, but the dappled, shifting, living light. That is what attention gives us. Not the whole truth, but the truth as it falls, in fragments, on the moving ground of our lives.

So I will try. I will try to notice the rain before it ends. I will listen to the sound of it, really listen, and let it saturate me like it saturates the earth. I will stand at the window a little longer. I will let the moment hold me, instead of trying to hold it.

Because the rain always stops. The light always moves. The leaves dry and the pavement fades back to grey. But the moment—if I am there for it—belongs to me. And I to it.
